questions.prompt: In "We Must Pace the Frontier" (September 2026), what did Dario Amodei propose, and what did Anthropic commit to unilaterally?

options.text: A full pause on frontier training; Anthropic committed to stop training new models.
options.rationale: The essay argues for slowing the rate of capability gains, not a halt.

options.text: A three-step plan (embedded third-party evaluators, coordination among frontier companies in democracies, then broader international coordination); Anthropic committed to the first step.
options.rationale: Yes. The unilateral commitment was ongoing, employee-like access for external evaluators.

options.text: Open-sourcing all frontier model weights to allow public auditing.
options.rationale: Not proposed in the essay.

options.text: A licensing regime run by the company's board.
options.rationale: Not proposed in the essay.

questions.explanation: The essay is notable because its premise (progress accelerated from mid-2026) is itself a factual claim you can check, and its first proposal is a verification mechanism, which is exactly what lesson 7 identifies as the weak point of voluntary frameworks.

questions.prompt: A colleague says Sam Altman's "The Gentle Singularity" was proven right because 2026 saw AI systems produce novel insights. How should you evaluate that?

options.text: Accept it; some AI-assisted research results appeared in 2026.
options.rationale: With an undefined target, almost any result can be counted, so this confirms little.

options.text: Point out that the prediction (systems that can figure out novel insights) was too loosely defined to fail; propose a checkable version and look for evidence on that instead.
options.rationale: Yes. Rewriting a claim until it can fail is the first step in scoring it.

options.text: Reject it; olympiad results do not count as insight.
options.rationale: That may be a reasonable definition, but you need to state it before scoring, not after.

questions.explanation: Soft predictions protect the forecaster and frustrate the reader. A useful response is a rewritten, dated claim plus the evidence that would settle it.

questions.code:
import math
now_h, target_h = 1.5, 40     # 80% horizon now, and a one-week target
for doubling_days in (89, 196):
    years = math.log2(target_h / now_h) * doubling_days / 365
    print(round(years, 1))

options.rationale: log2(40/1.5) is about 4.74 doublings; at 89 days that is 1.2 years, at 196 days 2.5 years.
That is the number of doublings, which does not depend on the doubling time.
That divides by the wrong constant; doublings times days, divided by 365.

questions.explanation: Even a one-week task at 80% reliability is one to two and a half years away on the trend, depending on which doubling time you believe. A single date hides that spread.

questions.prompt: Which statements correctly describe a critic's position as stated in their primary source? Select all that apply.

options.text: Yann LeCun argues that training mostly on text will not reach human-level intelligence and that world models learned from observation are needed.
options.rationale: Consistent with his 2022 position paper, his January 2026 Davos remarks, and his April 2026 Brown lecture.

options.text: Narayanan and Kapoor argue AI's economic effects will unfold over decades because adoption and diffusion are slow.
options.rationale: That is the core of "AI as Normal Technology" (April 2025).

options.text: Gary Marcus argued in 2022 that larger models would become more fluent without becoming correspondingly more trustworthy.
options.rationale: A central claim of "Deep Learning Is Hitting a Wall".

options.text: Narayanan and Kapoor claim AI models stopped improving in 2025.
options.rationale: Their argument is about diffusion and control, not a capability plateau.

questions.explanation: Critics are easy to misquote. Score them on what they actually wrote, and separate capability critiques (LeCun, Marcus) from impact critiques (Narayanan and Kapoor).

questions.prompt: What did METR's February 2026 update conclude about its developer productivity research?

options.text: That AI tools still slow experienced developers by about 19%.
options.rationale: That was the early-2025 result, which METR says is out of date.

options.text: That developers are probably sped up by current tools, but its new data were too affected by selection (developers unwilling to work without AI) to estimate by how much, so it is redesigning the study.
options.rationale: Yes. Its point estimates leaned toward speedups with intervals including zero.

options.text: That AI tools produce a reliable 10x speedup.
options.rationale: METR's 1.5x to 13x figure from staff transcripts was explicitly a soft upper bound.

options.text: That productivity cannot be measured.
options.rationale: METR proposed alternative designs rather than giving up.

questions.explanation: A trial can break when the treatment becomes too useful to give up. That is itself weak evidence of value, and a reason to design your own pilots carefully.

questions.prompt: A team lead uses this survey analysis to claim AI saved each engineer 8 hours a week. What is the main problem?
questions.code:
responses = survey("How many hours a week does AI save you?")
active = [r for r in responses if r.used_ai_last_week]
print("Average hours saved:", sum(r.hours for r in active) / len(active))

options.text: It averages self-reported savings from only the people who chose to answer and who used AI, with no measured comparison, so both the measurement and the sample are biased upward.
options.rationale: Yes. Self-reports overstate (METR 2025), and filtering to active users selects enthusiasts.

options.text: It should use the median instead of the mean.
options.rationale: A median would be more robust to outliers, but it does not fix self-report or selection bias.

options.text: Nothing; surveys are the standard way to measure productivity.
options.rationale: Surveys measure perception; decisions about headcount need measured outcomes.

questions.explanation: Measure outcomes (cycle time, accepted changes, defects) with a comparison, and use surveys for satisfaction and hypotheses.

questions.prompt: What did the August 2026 update of "Canaries in the Coal Mine?" (Stanford Digital Economy Lab) report?

options.text: Widespread layoffs across all AI-exposed occupations.
options.rationale: The authors report no widespread displacement.

options.text: No widespread job displacement, but employment of 22 to 25 year olds in the most AI-exposed occupations about 19% below trend, mainly through reduced hiring.
options.rationale: Yes. Occupations where AI complements workers showed flat or rising employment.

options.text: No measurable effect on any group.
options.rationale: The young-worker gap widened relative to the first version.

questions.explanation: Payroll data show where effects appear first: in hiring of entry-level workers in exposed jobs. That fits neither 'nothing is happening' nor 'jobs are disappearing broadly'.

questions.prompt: You are asked to brief leadership on whether to plan for "half of entry-level white-collar jobs disrupted within five years" (Amodei, January 2026). What is the best structure for the brief?

options.text: Quote the claim, list the arguments for, and recommend acting on it because the speaker has the best view of the technology.
options.rationale: One-sided, and access is not evidence.

options.text: Quote the full claim with its source and date; separate what is measured (hiring gaps for young workers, field productivity studies) from what is extrapolated; note incentives; give a probability range; and recommend low-regret actions (redesigning junior roles, measuring your own teams) plus the signals that would trigger bigger moves.
options.rationale: Yes. This is the claim-brief structure the project asks for.

options.text: Recommend ignoring it until it happens.
options.rationale: The evidence dilemma: waiting for certainty can leave you unprepared. Low-regret preparation is cheap.

questions.explanation: Good briefs make uncertainty actionable: what we know, what we do not, what we will do now regardless, and what would change the plan.

questions.prompt: Under the compounding-error argument, what does this print?

options.rationale: 0.95 to the 20th is about 0.36; to the 60th about 0.046.
Success must hold at every step, so probabilities multiply.
Small, but not zero.

questions.explanation: The argument is valid when steps fail independently and silently. Detectable failures with retries break the independence assumption, which is why verification matters more than raw per-step quality in long agent tasks.

questions.prompt: Which limitations apply to the Anthropic Economic Index as evidence about AI's economic effects? Select all that apply.

options.text: It is observational usage data, so it describes use rather than establishing what the tool causes.
options.rationale: The reports describe their measures as correlational.

options.text: Task success is the model's own assessment of conversations users chose to bring.
options.rationale: Stated in the January 2026 report.

options.text: It is published by a company with an interest in how AI's impact is perceived.
options.rationale: Context worth noting, even though the reports are careful about their limits.

options.text: It covers only a single user.
options.rationale: It covers millions of conversations; the limits are about representativeness and causation, not scale.

questions.explanation: Use provider data to understand patterns of use at scale, read their limitations sections, and look to experiments and labor data for effects.
